name: Speed work

card.summary: Submaximal lifting done with maximal bar speed, used by strength trainees to build power alongside strength and, through that, muscle and physique.

quick.overview:
Speed work, also called the dynamic effort method, means lifting submaximal weights while trying to move the bar as fast as possible. It comes from the Westside Barbell system created by Louie Simmons.
People use it to build power and strength as part of resistance training, which feeds the muscular physique many looksmaxxers want. The link to appearance is indirect.
quick.how: In the Westside system there are two dynamic effort sessions a week, one upper and one lower body, alternating with max effort sessions. Special exercises are rotated at least every three weeks.
quick.risks: As with any lifting, technique and load management matter. Specific harms for this method are not documented.

lead: Dynamic effort (speed work) is one of three training methods in the Westside Barbell system: sub-maximal weights moved with maximal speed.[1] Lifters accelerate as hard as they can through the upward phase of the lift.[1]

Louie Simmons (1947-2022), a powerlifter and coach who founded Westside Barbell in Columbus, Ohio, developed and popularised the approach, adapting Soviet and Bulgarian training protocols for powerlifting.[1]
People interested in physique may use it as one way to train strength and speed together each week, which can support heavier lifting and muscle building over time.[1]

chain: Builds power and strength alongside max effort work
Supports heavier training and more muscle
angle.text: Trainees run speed sessions to build strength and power each week; stronger lifters can train with heavier loads, which is how this connects to muscle growth.[1]

infobox: Two dynamic effort sessions weekly (upper, lower)

paras: The Westside system alternates two dynamic effort sessions with two max effort sessions per week, split between upper and lower body, as an alternative to traditional periodisation that develops a single quality at a time.[1]
The system is named after Westside Barbell and is sometimes called the Conjugate Method; it draws on Soviet conjugate sequencing that trained one main motor ability while maintaining others.[1]
